title: What is a Thread-Local Allocation Buffer (TLAB), and how does it make object allocation fast and lock-free in Eden?
shortTitle: What is a TLAB and how does it make allocation fast?

s1_definition.profdef: A Thread-Local Allocation Buffer, or TLAB, is a small private chunk of Eden that the JVM hands to an individual thread so that thread can allocate objects within it without coordinating with any other thread. Because each thread allocates from its own TLAB, the common case of object creation is just a bump of a pointer with no locking and no atomic operation, which makes allocation extremely fast. When a thread fills its TLAB, it atomically grabs a new chunk of Eden, and that is the only time it needs to synchronize.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Eden as a big shared ream of blank forms at National Bank of India, and many tellers all need forms at once. If every teller had to reach into the one shared pile for each form, they would constantly bump into each other and have to take turns, which is slow. Instead, each teller is handed their own small personal pad of forms (a TLAB). They tear off forms from their own pad as fast as they like, never waiting for anyone. Only when a teller's pad runs out do they briefly step to the central supply to grab a fresh pad, which is the one moment they coordinate. Most of the time, allocation is as quick as tearing off the next form.
s1_definition.oneliner: A TLAB is a thread's private slice of Eden, so allocating an object is usually just a lock-free pointer bump, and a thread only synchronizes when it needs a fresh TLAB.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A Thread-Local Allocation Buffer, or TLAB, is a small private chunk of Eden that the JVM hands to an individual thread so that thread can allocate objects within it without coordinating with any other thread. Because each thread allocates from its own TLAB, the common case of object creation is just a bump of a pointer with no locking and no atomic operation, which makes allocation extremely fast. When a thread fills its TLAB, it atomically grabs a new chunk of Eden, and that is the only time it needs to synchronize.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine Eden as a big shared ream of blank forms at National Bank of India, and many tellers all need forms at once. If every teller had to reach into the one shared pile for each form, they would constantly bump into each other and have to take turns, which is slow. Instead, each teller is handed their own small personal pad of forms (a TLAB). They tear off forms from their own pad as fast as they like, never waiting for anyone. Only when a teller's pad runs out do they briefly step to the central supply to grab a fresh pad, which is the one moment they coordinate. Most of the time, allocation is as quick as tearing off the next form.

**One line to remember:** A TLAB is a thread's private slice of Eden, so allocating an object is usually just a lock-free pointer bump, and a thread only synchronizes when it needs a fresh TLAB.

sections.s2_technical:
Eden is shared by all threads, and object creation is one of the most frequent operations in a running program, so if every allocation had to synchronize on the shared Eden it would become a severe bottleneck in a multi-threaded service. The TLAB mechanism removes that contention from the common path. When a thread needs to allocate, the JVM maintains for it a private region of Eden with two markers: a current pointer and an end pointer. Allocating an object of a given size is simply checking that the current pointer plus the size does not exceed the end pointer, placing the object at the current pointer, and advancing the current pointer by the size. This is called a bump-the-pointer allocation, and because the region belongs to only one thread, it needs no lock and no atomic compare-and-swap.

The only time a thread must coordinate is when its TLAB does not have enough room left for the next object. At that point the thread performs a single atomic operation to carve a fresh TLAB out of the shared Eden, advancing Eden's shared top pointer with a compare-and-swap. Because a TLAB is sized to hold many objects, this synchronized refill happens rarely compared to the number of allocations, so the amortized cost of allocation stays extremely low. The leftover space in a nearly full TLAB is either filled with a dummy object or retired so that Eden parsing during garbage collection stays correct.

There is a size consideration. If TLABs are too large, threads that allocate little waste Eden and trigger more frequent Minor GCs; if too small, threads refill too often and pay the synchronization cost more. The JVM sizes TLABs adaptively per thread based on each thread's recent allocation rate, so a hot allocating thread gets a bigger TLAB and a quiet thread gets a smaller one. You can observe and tune this with flags like `-XX:+UseTLAB`, which is on by default, and `-XX:TLABSize`, though in practice the adaptive sizing is good enough that you rarely touch it. A small banking example: a thread pool handling thousands of transfer requests per second allocates request and response objects almost entirely from TLABs, so allocation never becomes a contention point even under heavy concurrency.

A few senior nuances tie this to the bigger picture. First, objects larger than a TLAB, or larger than a fraction of it, are allocated directly in Eden or even straight into the Old generation rather than wasting a TLAB, which connects to the large-object promotion discussion. Second, TLABs are exactly why the generational copying collector's Eden allocation is so cheap: allocation is a pointer bump, and a Minor GC discards the whole Young generation at once, so neither allocation nor collection pays per-object overhead for the dead majority. Third, because TLAB allocation is thread-private, it also plays nicely with escape analysis and scalar replacement, where the JIT may avoid heap allocation altogether for objects that never escape a method, which is the next level of optimization beyond TLABs. The combination of per-thread bump allocation plus cheap young collection is a large part of why high-throughput Java services can allocate millions of short-lived objects per second without the allocation itself becoming a bottleneck.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India's transfer gateway runs many worker threads, each creating a burst of short-lived request and response objects. If every allocation contended on shared Eden, throughput would collapse under concurrency. This is exactly what TLABs solve, because each thread allocates from its own private slice of Eden with no locking.

Problem 2 — The team wanted to confirm that heavy concurrent allocation stayed fast and did not become a lock bottleneck. This is exactly what TLAB bump-pointer allocation guarantees, because threads only synchronize on the rare TLAB refill, not on each allocation.

In the mini-project we run many threads that each allocate large numbers of small transfer objects concurrently, measure total allocations and elapsed time to show throughput, and read the memory beans and a TLAB-related metric where available. The demo logs that concurrent allocation scales cleanly, illustrating the lock-free fast path.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile the demo
javac -d out src/main/java/com/bank/tlab/TlabDemo.java

# TLAB is ON by default; observe TLAB behavior with GC+TLAB logging
java -Xms512m -Xmx512m -XX:+UseTLAB -Xlog:gc+tlab=trace \
     -cp out com.bank.tlab.TlabDemo

# Contrast: disable TLAB to see allocation contention hurt multi-thread throughput
java -Xms512m -Xmx512m -XX:-UseTLAB \
     -cp out com.bank.tlab.TlabDemo
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: as many worker threads as processors, each allocating five million small transfer messages concurrently.

Step 1: The main thread logs the plan and submits one allocation worker per thread to the pool. Each worker will allocate its own burst of objects.

Step 2: Each worker begins creating TransferMessage objects. The JVM has given each thread its own TLAB, a private slice of Eden with a current pointer and an end pointer. Allocating a message is just placing it at the current pointer and advancing the pointer, with no lock.

Step 3: Because each thread bumps its own pointer, the threads never contend with each other on the common allocation path, so throughput scales with the number of cores rather than collapsing under lock contention.

Step 4: Periodically a worker fills its TLAB. Only then does it perform a single atomic operation to grab a fresh TLAB from shared Eden. Because each TLAB holds many objects, this refill is rare relative to the millions of allocations, so its cost is amortized away.

Step 5: Each message dies immediately after being used, so the Young generation stays full of garbage that cheap Minor GCs discard wholesale. The demo reports the total allocations and elapsed time, showing high throughput driven by lock-free TLAB allocation.

```text
[INFO] running 8 threads, each allocating 5000000 TransferMessages from its OWN TLAB
[INFO] allocated 40000000 objects in 310 ms
[INFO] throughput ≈ 129032 K allocations/sec per ms (no lock contention: each thread bumps its own TLAB pointer)
[INFO] only TLAB REFILL touches shared Eden (atomic, rare); checksum=...
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  Shared Eden
  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ [ TLAB-thread1 ][ TLAB-thread2 ][ TLAB-thread3 ] ...    │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
       │ each thread owns a private slice

  Thread 1 allocation (fast path, NO lock):
    check: current + size <= end ?
      YES → place object at current; current += size   (bump pointer)
      NO  → TLAB full → atomic CAS on Eden top → new TLAB (rare)

  Thread 2, 3, ... do the same IN PARALLEL on their OWN TLABs
    → no contention on the common path
    → only TLAB refill touches shared Eden atomically

  objects die young → Minor GC discards whole Young gen cheaply
```

```text
  ┌────────┐ REST ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │ Clients │────→│ Transfer Gateway          │
  └────────┘      │  thread pool (N workers)  │
                  │   each worker → own TLAB   │  lock-free alloc
                  │   short-lived req/resp     │
                  └───────────┬──────────────┘
                              ▼
                  ┌──────────────────────────┐
                  │ Young gen: Eden (TLABs)   │  bump-pointer, cheap Minor GC
                  └──────────────────────────┘
  Allocation never becomes a lock bottleneck under concurrency.
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — TLAB Mechanics ═══

  ┌─ Fast path (per thread, lock-free) ───────────────────┐
  │ TLAB = private Eden slice: [start .. current .. end]  │
  │ allocate(size):                                        │
  │   if current + size <= end:                            │
  │       obj = current; current += size; return obj       │  bump pointer
  │   else: refillTLAB()   ← slow path                     │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ Slow path (rare, synchronized) ──────────────────────┐
  │ refillTLAB(): atomic CAS to advance Eden's shared top  │
  │   → carve a new TLAB (sized by adaptive policy)        │
  │   retire old TLAB remainder (dummy fill for parsing)   │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Sizing: adaptive per thread by recent allocation rate
    too big → wasted Eden, more Minor GC
    too small → frequent refills, more CAS
  Flags: -XX:+UseTLAB (default on), -XX:TLABSize (rarely tuned)

  Big-object rule: object > TLAB (or > fraction) → allocated
    directly in Eden / Old gen (no TLAB waste)
  Synergy: escape analysis + scalar replacement may avoid heap
    allocation entirely for non-escaping objects.
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A Thread-Local Allocation Buffer, or TLAB, is a small private chunk of Eden that the JVM hands to an individual thread so that thread can allocate objects within it without coordinating with any other thread. This matters because Eden is shared by all threads and object creation is one of the most frequent operations in a running program, so if every single allocation had to synchronize on the shared Eden, it would become a severe bottleneck in any multi-threaded service. The TLAB mechanism removes that contention from the common path entirely.

The way it works is that the JVM maintains for each thread a private region of Eden with two markers, a current pointer and an end pointer. Allocating an object is just checking that the current pointer plus the object's size does not exceed the end pointer, placing the object at the current pointer, and advancing that pointer by the size. This is called bump-the-pointer allocation, and because the region belongs to exactly one thread, it needs no lock and no atomic compare-and-swap. That is why allocation in Java is so cheap on the fast path: it is essentially a pointer increment.

The only time a thread must coordinate with others is when its TLAB runs out of room for the next object. At that moment the thread performs a single atomic operation to carve a fresh TLAB out of the shared Eden, advancing Eden's shared top pointer with a compare-and-swap. Because a TLAB is sized to hold many objects, this synchronized refill is rare compared to the number of allocations, so the amortized cost of allocation stays extremely low. The JVM even sizes TLABs adaptively per thread based on recent allocation rate, so a hot allocating thread gets a bigger TLAB and a quiet one gets a smaller one, and this is all on by default under the UseTLAB flag so I rarely tune it. In my banking work, a transfer gateway with a thread pool handling thousands of requests per second allocates request and response objects almost entirely from TLABs, so allocation never becomes a contention point even under heavy concurrency.

The senior nuances I like to connect are three. First, objects too large for a TLAB are allocated directly in Eden or straight into the Old generation rather than wasting a buffer, which ties into the large-object promotion story. Second, TLABs are exactly why generational copying collection is so efficient overall: allocation is a lock-free pointer bump and a Minor GC throws away the whole Young generation at once, so neither allocation nor collection pays per-object overhead for the dead majority. Third, because TLAB allocation is thread-private, it composes beautifully with escape analysis and scalar replacement, where the JIT can avoid heap allocation altogether for objects that never escape a method. Together, per-thread bump allocation and cheap young collection are a big part of why high-throughput Java services can create millions of short-lived objects per second without the allocation itself ever becoming the bottleneck.

---

keyPoints: TLAB: Thread-Local Allocation Buffer — private Eden region per thread
Allocation is pointer-bump: just move the pointer, no locking
Each thread allocates from its own TLAB — zero contention
When TLAB fills, thread gets a new one (small synchronization)
Result: object allocation is nearly as fast as stack allocation
